title: A 'Challenging but Exciting Time' for the Legal Profession, Says Wilkins
author: David B. Wilkins

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: Wilkins identifies client pressure for firms to use AI to streamline work and reduce fees, but offers only a forecast of buyer pressure. He does not address the cluster’s central claims about multidisciplinary implementation, substantive verification, task-specific evaluation or demonstrated service reliability.
qs: This means that while law firms are paying huge salaries to acquire or retain star partners, they are also likely to face pressure by general counsels to use AI and other technologies to reduce fees and streamline work.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: Wilkins accepts that AI may compress routine junior work and reduce entry-level hiring without implying profession-wide employment collapse. He materially extends the cluster by emphasizing technology-integrating skills and AI-generated legal demand as countervailing forces, though he does not directly analyze leverage, revenue or apprenticeship.
qs: Nevertheless, law firms and other employers will certainly look at these tools as creating the potential for reducing entry-level hiring, given that much of the day-to-day work of entry-level lawyers — document review, drafting, legal research — can now be done increasingly well by AI.

The same is true of AI, which at least in the short term is likely to be a welfare act for lawyers, as everything from disputes over intellectual property, liability for hallucinations, and the reach and interpretation of new AI regulations will be litigated on all sides.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: Wilkins accepts the core reconfiguration thesis: technology enables new providers to capture standardised work and intensifies competition with traditional firms. He materially extends the cluster beyond corporate workflow allocation by highlighting direct-to-consumer services and regulatory reform as additional mechanisms enabling new delivery models, while remaining cautious about the Big Four’s eventual success.
qs: On the other we are already seeing a number of tech startups offering DIY services directly to consumers in areas such as wills, real estate, and even fighting parking tickets that have traditionally been handled by these kinds of firms.

st.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform
st.an: Wilkins supports the cluster’s core proposition that AI-era legal development should preserve foundational legal analysis while broadening competence to include problem-solving, empathy and interdisciplinary collaboration. He also endorses selective reform of training and work models, though this source does not develop the cluster’s specific proposals on lifelong coordination, funding apprenticeship or AI verification.
qs: But thinking like a lawyer has to be thinking like a problem solver.
At the same time, we still have to train students around the fundamental ideas of legal analysis and legal interpretation and legal writing.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Wilkins supports the cluster’s central account of task-level reconfiguration rather than wholesale lawyer replacement. He identifies entry-level research, drafting and document review as increasingly automatable, while arguing that technology-enabled problem solving can sustain lawyer demand. He also reinforces the need for educational preparation, though he does not substantially address verification or apprenticeship design.
qs: Nevertheless, law firms and other employers will certainly look at these tools as creating the potential for reducing entry-level hiring, given that much of the day-to-day work of entry-level lawyers — document review, drafting, legal research — can now be done increasingly well by AI.
The future is not machines instead of people.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: Wilkins aligns closely with the synthesis: he identifies routine entry-level work as the principal employment risk while rejecting dramatic overall hiring decline as inevitable. He expects restructuring around technology-integrated skills, new legal demand, value-based billing and redesigned training rather than wholesale elimination of lawyers. His claims are primarily qualitative forecasts, not measured evidence of displacement.
qs: Nevertheless, law firms and other employers will certainly look at these tools as creating the potential for reducing entry-level hiring, given that much of the day-to-day work of entry-level lawyers — document review, drafting, legal research — can now be done increasingly well by AI.
This doesn't mean, however, that overall hiring will fall dramatically if law students who come into legal organizations bring other kinds of skills that create value.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Wilkins supports the cluster’s core proposition that AI will reorganise legal-service production, competition and pricing rather than simply eliminate lawyers. He particularly reinforces the conflict between AI-enabled efficiency and hourly billing, while preserving a central role for human creativity, empathy and professionalism. His forecasts about startups, ALSPs and regulatory liberalisation are directionally consistent with the cluster but less qualified by evidence of current scale.
qs: How can humans work with machines while preserving core human values like creativity, empathy, and professionalism?

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Wilkins directly supports the cluster’s central proposition: AI may substitute for routine junior legal tasks and reduce entry-level hiring incentives, while complementary skills and new sources of legal demand may sustain broader employment. His claims are qualified predictions rather than measured evidence of aggregate displacement.
qs: Nevertheless, law firms and other employers will certainly look at these tools as creating the potential for reducing entry-level hiring, given that much of the day-to-day work of entry-level lawyers — document review, drafting, legal research — can now be done increasingly well by AI.
This doesn't mean, however, that overall hiring will fall dramatically if law students who come into legal organizations bring other kinds of skills that create value.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Wilkins accepts the cluster’s central work-redesign proposition: AI should reshape human-led legal work while preserving professional judgment and values. His claims about productivity, value-based pricing and changing provider competition align with the cluster’s account of task reallocation and business-model pressure, although he does not materially address jagged capability, verification or use-context evaluation.
qs: How can we rethink our understanding of "work," and how can we build vibrant and inclusive workplaces that are both efficient and sustainable?
How can humans work with machines while preserving core human values like creativity, empathy, and professionalism?

kp.k: Automation threatens entry-level tasks, not necessarily overall hiring
kp.d: Wilkins asserts that legal automation is already occurring and predicts acceleration in the coming year and beyond. He expects employers to consider reducing entry-level hiring because AI increasingly performs document review, drafting and research, but conditions his more optimistic overall hiring outlook on entrants contributing technology-enabled, sophisticated problem-solving skills. These are interview assessments rather than measured employment findings; he situates automation historically by recalling restrictions on first-year students using Lexis and Westlaw when he began teaching in 1986.
qs: Nevertheless, law firms and other employers will certainly look at these tools as creating the potential for reducing entry-level hiring, given that much of the day-to-day work of entry-level lawyers — document review, drafting, legal research — can now be done increasingly well by AI.
This doesn't mean, however, that overall hiring will fall dramatically if law students who come into legal organizations bring other kinds of skills that create value.
The future is not machines instead of people. It's people who know how to use and work with technology to help address increasingly difficult and complex problems.

kp.k: Government cuts independently pressure legal employment
kp.d: Wilkins distinguishes technological displacement from political and fiscal pressures. He reports federal job cuts since January 20, including legal-sector positions, and suggests some jobs may move to state and local government, while noting financial constraints there and among government-funded NGOs. He predicts private-sector spillovers alongside additional work contesting presidential actions.
qs: Of course, much of the pressure on entry-level hiring — and hiring in general — has nothing to do with technology.
Since January 20, President Donald Trump and Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency have slashed jobs across the federal government, including many in the legal sector.
Some of these jobs may move to state and local governments, but these sectors are also under tremendous financial pressure, as are NGOs that rely on government funding.

kp.k: AI disputes could generate new specialist legal work
kp.d: Wilkins predicts that, at least in the short term, disputes about intellectual property, liability for hallucinations and AI regulation will generate legal demand. He expects more firms to establish specialized practices addressing these disputes; he does not quantify the resulting employment or revenue.
qs: The same is true of AI, which at least in the short term is likely to be a welfare act for lawyers, as everything from disputes over intellectual property, liability for hallucinations, and the reach and interpretation of new AI regulations will be litigated on all sides.
This is why we are going to see more and more law firms creating specialized practice areas dedicated to handling these kinds of disputes.

kp.k: Smaller firms face productivity gains and consumer-service competition
kp.d: Wilkins describes small and medium-sized firms using technology to expand lawyers' productive capacity while startups offer consumers DIY services in wills, real estate and parking-ticket disputes. He predicts significant startup growth in the coming year as AI accuracy and usability improve. His capacity argument concerns productivity, not a stated change in associate-to-partner staffing ratios.
qs: On the one hand, small and medium-sized law firms are already increasingly turning to technology to "leverage up" the capacity of their lawyers to be more productive in ways that make them more competitive.

On the other we are already seeing a number of tech startups offering DIY services directly to consumers in areas such as wills, real estate, and even fighting parking tickets that have traditionally been handled by these kinds of firms.
As technology improves both the ease of use and accuracy of AI tools, the number of such startups is likely to grow significantly in the coming year.

kp.k: Regulatory experimentation may expand nontraditional legal provision
kp.d: Wilkins identifies unauthorized-practice and outside-investment restrictions as obstacles to new providers. He cites experimental licensing in Arizona and New Mexico as pressure for wider liberalization and Arizona's permission for KPMG to practice law as an example of potential employment consequences. He predicts the other Big Four will follow and that ALSPs will compete for talent and clients in the coming year, while expressly leaving the Big Four's eventual success unresolved.
qs: And while rules against unauthorized practice and outside investment still remain a challenge for these companies, the willingness of states like Arizona and New Mexico to license experimental models in their regulatory "sandboxes" will continue to put pressure on other states and the American Bar Association to loosen these restrictions.

The fact that Arizona granted KPMG, one of the Big Four professional services companies, permission to practice law in the state — with the other three surely to follow — underscores how these regulatory reforms might affect legal employment.

Although the jury is still out on how successful the Big Four will be in their latest attempt to enter the legal market, there seems little doubt that they and a number of other so-called "alternative legal service providers" such as investigation firms, managed services companies, and legal process outsourcers, will actively compete with law firms and other traditional providers for both talent and clients in the coming year.

kp.k: Partner mobility amplifies political and competitive market instability
kp.d: Wilkins reports escalating bidding for partners with substantial client business in early 2025, including multiyear salary guarantees. He argues that threatened or actual executive restrictions impede transactional work, expose affected firms to partner and client departures, and help explain some firms' agreements with President Trump. He further argues that these dynamics destabilize legal markets and complicate companies' investment decisions by raising uncertainty over access to preferred counsel.
qs: Already in the first few months of the year, we have seen the bidding war for top partners continue to escalate, as firms try to lure lawyers who have large "books of business" with eyepopping salaries (many of which are now guaranteed for several years) as a way of entering new markets or increasing their profitability.
Indeed, the threat of losing superstar partners, particularly in transactional areas, is one of the factors that has led several leading law firms to negotiate deals with President Trump.
Law firms that lose partners and clients in this way risk "unraveling" as other partners and clients quickly head for the door in search of safer (and greener) pastures.

kp.k: Buyer pressure pushes AI efficiency and value-based billing
kp.d: Wilkins contrasts rising star-partner compensation with general counsels' pressure to reduce spending. He predicts clients will push firms to use AI and other technologies to streamline work and lower fees, and argues that firms consequently need to charge for the value produced rather than time spent. This is a forecast and pricing prescription, not evidence of measured adoption of alternative fee arrangements.
qs: At the same time, general counsels are under increasing pressure to reduce costs.

This means that while law firms are paying huge salaries to acquire or retain star partners, they are also likely to face pressure by general counsels to use AI and other technologies to reduce fees and streamline work.
You cannot bill for AI by the hour. Lawyers will need to find ways to bill clients on the basis of the value that their legal work creates as opposed to the time it took to produce it.

kp.k: Hybrid workplaces require deliberate culture and developmental justification
kp.d: Wilkins predicts conflict over workplace policies and observes a backlash against remote work. Rather than claiming collaboration requires office attendance, he recommends intentional culture-building in hybrid workplaces and asks advocates of returning to the office to demonstrate concrete benefits for workers' professional development and personal growth.
qs: There's been an increasing backlash against remote policies.

Now, that doesn't mean you can't do these things, but it does mean that employers and employees must be much more intentional in their efforts to create a vibrant and stable culture in the new hybrid workplace.
And it can't just be "that's the way I did it," or "that's the way people have always learned," but tied to real and tangible benefits for professional development and personal growth.

kp.k: Retention requires institutional trust, not simply higher compensation
kp.d: Wilkins asserts that chronic departures particularly affect women, people of color and other traditional outsiders, and argues that increasing pay has diminishing effectiveness. He links younger workers' distrust to experiences of the pandemic, two recessions, burnout and layoffs. He explicitly presents repairing institutional trust as a hope rather than a prediction, alongside a call to rethink sustainable workplaces, human-machine collaboration, training and incentives for innovation.
qs: It is no secret that there is a chronic exodus of people leaving the profession, particularly women, people of color, and other traditional outsiders.
And the people at the top have been trying to make up for it simply by paying more money.
How can humans work with machines while preserving core human values like creativity, empathy, and professionalism?
Right now, trust has been broken in lots of different ways, and one of our major tasks — this is not so much a prediction as a hope — is to begin to work actively and consciously to repair trust.

kp.k: Legal education must combine fundamentals with interdisciplinary problem-solving
kp.d: Wilkins argues that technological change, geopolitical tensions, expanding law and regulation, and misinformation require a broader conception of thinking like a lawyer. He recommends empathy, collaborative problem-solving across perspectives, and the ability to contribute without always leading. He calls for recruiting students from varied backgrounds and enabling open disagreement to overcome knowledge and relationship silos, while retaining legal analysis, interpretation and writing.
qs: Thinking like a lawyer is more important than ever. But thinking like a lawyer has to be thinking like a problem solver.
It has to be thinking about being an empathetic listener.
It's being a member of the team, not always leading the team.
Law schools have to teach their students to recognize these silos — and then how to break through them.
At the same time, we still have to train students around the fundamental ideas of legal analysis and legal interpretation and legal writing.

kp.k: Novel problems create opportunities for junior lawyers' expertise
kp.d: Wilkins reports a managing partner's observation that current problems lack established experts, then argues that novel challenges allow expertise to come from across seniority levels rather than solely through traditional progression. He recommends teaching students that technological knowledge and cross-cultural fluency can make their contributions immediately relevant despite instability.
qs: A managing partner of a law firm recently said to me, "It's a tough time for junior lawyers." But, he said, "You know what? The problems we're grappling with now, there are no experts."
In this world, expertise can and should come from everywhere.

As law schools, we should be teaching students that, while the instability all around them can be scary, it also means that their ideas and unique expertise around things like technology and cross-cultural fluency are more important and relevant than ever.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Wilkins predicts accelerating automation and potential reductions in entry-level hiring, but not necessarily a dramatic decline in overall hiring.
pts.d: David Wilkins, the interviewed speaker, says AI increasingly performs document review, drafting and legal research, giving employers reasons to consider hiring fewer entry-level lawyers. He qualifies this prediction: graduates who combine technology with sophisticated problem-solving can create other value and remain in demand. His preferred future is human–technology collaboration rather than wholesale replacement. He separately identifies government cuts and funding pressures as non-technological causes of hiring pressure, so his account does not attribute all employment changes to AI.

pts.k: Wilkins predicts that AI will also generate legal work and specialized dispute practices.
pts.d: He expects litigation concerning intellectual property, liability for AI hallucinations, and the interpretation and scope of AI regulation to increase demand for lawyers, at least in the short term. This is a prediction about new legal demand, not a quantified estimate of whether new work will offset automated work.

pts.k: Wilkins describes technology as both a productivity aid and a source of direct competition for smaller firms.
pts.d: Small and medium-sized firms can use technology to expand lawyers' productive capacity and competitiveness. At the same time, consumer-facing DIY startups compete in services such as wills, real estate and parking-ticket challenges. Wilkins predicts significant startup growth as AI becomes easier to use and more accurate. His phrase 'leverage up' concerns productive capacity here; he offers no claim about a change in associate-to-partner staffing ratios.

pts.k: Wilkins links technology-enabled entry to regulatory change and wider competition from nontraditional legal providers.
pts.d: He says unauthorized-practice and outside-investment restrictions remain obstacles to consumer-facing startups, while experimental licensing models put pressure on states and the ABA to relax restrictions. As an adjacent legal-market development, he cites Arizona's permission for KPMG to practice law and predicts entry by the other Big Four firms and competition from ALSPs for talent and clients. He does not establish that AI causes Big Four entry, and explicitly leaves their eventual success uncertain.

pts.k: Wilkins predicts client pressure to use AI will force firms to rethink hourly billing in favor of value-based pricing.
pts.d: He links general counsels' cost pressures to demands that outside firms streamline work and reduce fees through AI and other technologies. He argues firms will need to charge for the value created rather than production time. This is a forward-looking business-model claim, not evidence that hourly billing has already disappeared. He places it within broader market pressures, including expensive partner recruitment, that he expects to increase volatility.

pts.k: Wilkins argues that technology increases the importance of interdisciplinary, collaborative problem-solving and creates opportunities for younger lawyers.
pts.d: His educational prescription is to supplement, not abandon, foundational legal analysis, interpretation and writing with technological integration, empathy, collaboration and cross-cultural fluency. He situates this shift within technological and geopolitical uncertainty rather than treating it as exclusively AI-driven. He argues novel problems make junior lawyers' distinctive expertise more relevant. These are professional and educational judgments, not measured findings about graduate outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest primarily on Wilkins's expert judgment, qualitative observations and selected examples, not quantitative research presented in the interview.
pts.d: The source identifies Wilkins as a Harvard law professor and faculty director of the Center on the Legal Profession. For automation, he offers a historical recollection of legal research technology and asserts current AI capabilities without benchmarks. For smaller-firm competition, he describes adoption and DIY offerings without naming firms or presenting market data. For regulatory change, he cites experimental licensing and KPMG's Arizona permission. The litigation, hiring, pricing and educational predictions receive explanatory reasoning but no numerical forecasts, cited studies or measured outcomes. No specific hallucination sanctions case or hallucination-rate study is supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Near-term predictions are anchored to the April 15, 2025 interview, while educational and professional changes have a broader horizon.
pts.d: Automation is described as already occurring and accelerating 'in the coming year and beyond.' Startup growth and ALSP competition are forecast for the coming year, without a precise endpoint. Additional AI litigation demand is qualified as occurring 'at least in the short term.' Hiring resilience depends on entrants bringing value beyond automated tasks; startup growth depends on improved AI usability and accuracy, with regulatory barriers remaining. Big Four success is expressly uncertain. The pricing shift has no specific completion date. Educational reform is an ongoing prescription within a longer-term rethinking of the profession.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects differ across entrants to the profession, law-firm segments, alternative providers, buyers and educators.
pts.d: Entry-level lawyers face automation of common assignments and possible hiring reductions, while technology-capable problem solvers may retain strong demand. Law firms gain potential AI-disputes work but face client pressure over efficiency and fees. Small and medium-sized firms gain capacity while confronting consumer DIY competition. Consumers encounter alternative ways to handle routine matters; the source does not measure affordability or access-to-justice outcomes. The Big Four and other ALSPs compete for clients and talent. General counsels act as cost-conscious buyers pushing change in outside firms. Law schools must prepare students to integrate technology with core legal skills, collaboration and empathy; clients, governments, NGOs and nonprofits are identified as beneficiaries of that problem-solving capability.
